**Subsection 1 — A₁→A₂: The Actualization of Perception (~400 words).**
Declare the architectural role. A₁→A₂ is the perceptual motion whose unmoved originator is the sensible object in actuality (inherited from A₁'s preconditions), whose moved mover is the sense faculty in its first actuality, and whose terminus A₂ is the completed perceptual act. State that this section proceeds by (a) specifying the A₁ preconditions, (b) developing Aristotle's hylomorphic account of form-reception, (c) applying the three-factor kinetic schema from A₀ to perception, (d) analyzing perception as enmattered *alloiosis*, (e) defining the residual motion (resonant *kinesis*) that persists in the sense-organ after the perceptual act, and (f) arguing that this residue has a dual structure: resonant *aisthēma* (formal-epistemic trace) and resonant *orexis* (affective-orectic trace). Cross-reference: *see the prior section on A₀ for the motion-and-time framework that grounds this analysis.*

**Subsection 2 — The Preconditions: A₁ and the Medium (~500 words).**
Specify what must already be actual for perception to occur. Two preconditions: (i) the sensible quality actually exercises its power (the color is visible, the sound audible); (ii) the sense-organ holds its first actuality as capacity to receive the sensible form. Develop the role of the medium — *Sense and Sensibilia* 6, 447a3-7 on the sequential affection of the medium ("each part of it successively is affected by the part contiguous") and *Sense and Sensibilia* 6, 446b8-9 on light as the exception to sequential transmission. Note that the medium's sequential affection is the physical correlate of the temporal horizon A₀ establishes. A₁ inherits its intelligibility from A₀: motion and time being already actual is what allows the sensible object to exercise its power through the medium and the sense-organ to be prepared to receive it.

**Subsection 3 — Hylomorphism and the Reception of Form (~700 words).**
Develop Aristotle's account of perception as the reception of sensible form without matter. DEPLOY *De Anima* II.12, 424a17-24 EARLY as the decisive textual warrant — the wax-signet-ring metaphor: "a sense is what has the power of receiving into itself the sensible forms of things without the matter, in the way in which a piece of wax takes on the impress of a signet-ring without the iron or gold." Argue that the sense-organ undergoes a formal (not material) alteration. Integrate *De Anima* II.12, 424a24-29 on the sense-organ as spatial magnitude but the sensory power itself as "a certain form or power in a magnitude." Develop the "sense as ratio (*logos*)" thesis at *De Anima* III.2, 426a27-b8: each sense is constituted by a proportion between the contraries proper to its domain (hot/cold, bitter/sweet), and perceptible qualities are themselves ratios of their underlying contraries. Use the signet-ring example as an extended illustration. Discuss the destruction condition: if the sensible exceeds the ratio of the organ, the motion acts on the organ *as matter* rather than *as sense*, and the ratio is destroyed (the perceptual act never reaches A₂). This is a "failed actualization" rather than an absence of motion.

**Subsection 4 — The Activity of Mover and Moved as One (~500 words).**
Apply the three-factor kinetic schema from A₀ to perception. The unmoved originator is the sensible object in actuality; the moved mover is the sense faculty; that which is moved is the perceiver via the sense-organ. Deploy *Physics* III.2, 202a13-20 ("there is a single actuality of both alike") to argue that the actuality of the sensible object and the actuality of the sense faculty are numerically one event. Deploy *De Anima* III.2, 425b26-27: "the activity of the sensible object and that of sense is one and the same activity, and yet the distinction between their being remains." Use *De Anima* III.2, 425b28-426a1 (hearkening and sounding): "when that which can hear is actively hearing and that which can sound is sounding, then the actual hearing and the actual sound come about at the same time." The perceptual event is analogical unity: one in substrate, two in being. Note: the sense faculty as "moved mover" is an analogical extension of *DA* III.10 433b10-18 (originally specified for locomotive action); the perceptual case is structurally analogous but not strictly isomorphic — the actualization of the sense faculty *is* the actualization of the organ's capacity under the same description. Cross-reference *De Anima* II.12, 424a17-24 and the A₀ section's three-factor treatment.

**Subsection 5 — Perception as Enmattered Alloiosis (~500 words).**
Develop perception as a qualitative change (*alloiōsis*). Cite *De Anima* II.5, 416b33-417a1: "Sensation depends, as we have said, on a process of movement or affection from without, for it is held to be some sort of change in quality." Distinguish two kinds of *alloiōsis* per *De Anima* II.5: ordinary qualitative change (corruption) versus preservation (the actualization of a potentiality brought to its proper fulfillment). Perception is the second kind: the sense-organ is "preserved" in its actualization, not corrupted. Kevin White's reading illuminates the ontological specificity of this. The *pathos* in the sense-organ is formally — not materially — identical to the sensible quality: the wax takes the signet's form without the iron, just as the eye takes the color without becoming colored as matter. Then transition: if perception is an *alloiōsis* that preserves rather than corrupts, and if the sense-organ is formally altered without being materially altered, then the motion must persist in some mode after the sensible object withdraws — otherwise the sensible form it has received would vanish with the object.

**Subsection 6 — Resonant Kinesis: The Persisting Impression (~800 words).**
Establish that the perceptual motion does not simply cease when the sensible object departs; it persists as a residual motion in the sensory apparatus. Deploy *De Anima* III.2, 425b23-26: "That is why even when the sensible objects are gone the sensings and imaginings continue to exist in the sense-organs." Deploy *On Dreams* 2, 459a24-28: "The objects of sense-perception corresponding to each sensory organ produce sense-perception in us, and the affection due to their operation is present in the organs of sense not only when the perceptions are actualized, but even when they have departed." Deploy *On Dreams* 2, 459b1-6 on the physical analogy: just as heat remains in water after the fire is removed, so the physical motions of perception remain in the sensory organs after the object is gone. Deploy *On Dreams* 2, 460b2-3 where Aristotle names these residual impressions *aisthēmata*. Introduce the coinage **resonant *kinesis*** for this residual motion: the persisting vibration within the sensory apparatus. Develop the signet-ring anatomy: (a) Potentiality — the wax pliable and the ring held above it; (b) Actualization — the ring presses into the wax and the pathos is impressed (the actualization ends when the ring is removed); (c) Residual Trace — the wax has undergone *alloiōsis* of the preservative kind, and the impression persists after the ring has departed. Argue that this residual motion is what distinguishes the living soul from a merely physical medium that ceases to be affected once the stimulus is withdrawn. Cite White on resonant reverberation: the living soul "carries the reverberating effects of its past encounters with sensible objects; it is not only a receiver, but also a preserver and storehouse, of the sensible forms of things" (White, "The Meaning of *Phantasia* in Aristotle's *De Anima*, III, 3-8," p. 498). Note that Aristotle himself uses no single technical term for this residual motion; "resonant *kinesis*" is introduced here as a coinage to mark its ongoing character and its structural role as the material cause of *phantasmata* at the next stage (A₃).

**Subsection 7 — The Dual-Trace Thesis: Resonant Aisthēma and Resonant Orexis (~1,000 words).**
This is the section's most philosophically consequential move. Argue that the residual motion (resonant *kinesis*) is not a single undifferentiated trace but a composite whose internal duality is formally distinct in two aspects: (a) **resonant *aisthēma*** — the formal-epistemic content (the "what it is" of the perceived object: the residual shape, color, sound, or smell); and (b) **resonant *orexis*** — the affective-orectic trace (the pleasure/pain valence, the pursue/avoid orientation that accompanied the original perceptual act).

Structure the argument as two converging proofs:

(A) **Analytic entailment from perception to valence.** Deploy *De Anima* II.3, 414b1-6: "whatever has a sense has the capacity for pleasure and pain and therefore has pleasant and painful objects present to it, and wherever these are present, there is desire, for desire is appetition of what is pleasant." This is a chain of analytic entailments: sensation → pleasure/pain capacity → pleasant/painful objects present → appetite. Every act of sensation therefore analytically entails affective valence; sensation without such valence is a contradiction in terms. Deploy *De Anima* III.7, 431a8-14: "To perceive then is like bare asserting or thinking; but when the object is pleasant or painful, the soul makes a sort of affirmation or negation, and pursues or avoids the object." Emphasize the decisive qualification Aristotle adds: "the faculty of appetite and avoidance are not different, either from one another or from the faculty of sense-perception; but their being is different" — numerically one in substrate, two in being. Apply this formula: the residual motion that persists after the object departs inherits the same structure — numerically one affection, formally dual.

(B) **Modus tollens from motivational inertness.** If the residual affection were exhausted by the formal-epistemic trace (the resonant *aisthēma* alone), then mere retention of sensible form would suffice to originate pursuit and avoidance — the knowledge *that the object is a wolf* would, by itself, move the animal to flee. But *De Anima* III.7, 431a8-14 insists that bare perception is "like bare asserting or thinking"; only *when the object is pleasant or painful* does the soul pursue or avoid. Hence the formal-epistemic content alone is motivationally inert; a distinct operation — the hedonic-orectic valuation — is required. If the residual affection were exhausted by the formal trace, the affective residue would have no independent operative force. But *On Dreams* 2, 460b4-11 (the cowardly, erotic, angry deceived by slight resemblances) shows that affective residue does modulate the threshold of formal recognition — the coward's existing fear primes recognition of enemies with minimal formal similarity. And *MA* 7, 702a17-19 specifies that "the organic parts are suitably prepared by the affections, these again by desire, and desire by imagination" — inserting *pathē* as a distinct causal step between desire and the organic parts. If the affective dimension were simply identical with the formal content, its insertion as a distinct causal step would be otiose. Therefore the residual affection harbors an internal duality.

Supplementary evidence: deploy *Rhetoric* I.11, 1370a27-b1 on pleasure as a kind of weak perception that attends remembering and expecting. The pleasure that attaches to memory is not a new judgment about the past; it is a residual affection carried by *phantasia* as part of its content — direct evidence that affective valence persists alongside the formal trace and is delivered by the residual motion without an intervening evaluative act. Deploy *De Anima* I.1, 403a25-b19 on *pathē* as "enmattered accounts": the definition of any affection combines formal account (what it is *about*) and material account (the bodily state in which it is realized). The enmattered-accounts framework supplies the hylomorphic warrant: since the residual motion is an enmattered composite, and the composite has distinguishable formal and material aspects, the formal-epistemic and affective-orectic dimensions are distinct formal aspects of a single substrate. They are one in substrate, different in being — the same formula Aristotle applies to perception and appetite at 431a13-14.

Close the argument by stating the dual structure: resonant *kinesis* is the residual motion as a whole; resonant *aisthēma* is the formal-epistemic imprint ("what the object is"); resonant *orexis* is the affective-orectic imprint ("what the object means for pursuit or avoidance"). These are one in substrate, different in being, mapped respectively onto the perceptual faculty (retaining the sensible form) and the appetitive faculty (retaining the pleasure or pain). Aristotle himself does not name the second trace; his commitments — that sensation entails valence, that valence is formally distinct from epistemic content, that the whole affection persists, and that the affective dimension has its own causal efficacy — collectively require it.

**Subsection 8 — Synthesis: A₂ as Ground of A₃ (~400 words).**
Close the section by stating A₂'s architectural role. A₂ is the completed perceptual actuality: the joint actualization of sensible object and sense faculty terminating in the reception of form without matter. A₂'s content — the dual-trace composite of resonant *aisthēma* and resonant *orexis* — serves as the unmoved originator of the next motion in the chain: the phantastic motion M₂→A₃ through which the residual trace is activated by *phantasia* and crystallized into the *phantasma* proper. Deposit the reader at the threshold of A₃ with a sentence flagging the genetic relationship: just as A₀'s motion and time grounded A₁'s preconditions and A₁ grounded A₂'s perceptual event, so A₂'s residual trace grounds A₃'s phantasmatic image. The chain is iterative and nested — each completed actuality is simultaneously the terminus of its antecedent motion and the unmoved originator of its successor. Attach the Heidegger deferral footnote specified above.

**Development Note (~300 words, own `\subsection*{Development Note}` AFTER subsection 8).**
Flag for future development: (i) the question whether every sensory affection inherits *both* traces in all animals, or whether certain organisms might retain only the formal aspect without the orectic valence, is textually underdetermined in Aristotle but bears on the wider thesis about appetite as the single source of animal movement; (ii) the precise mechanism by which the sense-organ's sequential affection through the medium translates into the unified perceptual act is not fully articulated in *De Anima* and requires supplementary analysis from *Sense and Sensibilia* and the *De Motu Animalium*; (iii) the relationship between resonant *orexis* and what Aristotle calls *pathē* in the Rhetoric's catalogue of higher-order emotions (anger, fear, pity, shame) — which operate only in rational animals capable of *doxa* — must be distinguished from the basic affective valence co-constitutive with perception at A₂ (this is the distinction between *pathos* simpliciter and *pathē* in the higher-order sense that the downstream sections on cognitive actualities and emotion will develop).

# A₁→A₂: The Actualization of Perception

## 1. A₁→A₂: The Actualization of Perception

The preceding section established that motion and time constitute A₀, the ground-level actuality from which every subsequent stage of the perceptual chain arises. Motion, understood as the fulfilment of what is potentially insofar as it is potential, provides the ontological scaffold upon which the ensouled body first encounters the sensible world; time, as the number of motion with respect to the before and after, supplies the continuous metric within which successive actualizations can be ordered and distinguished (Aristotle, *Physics*, p. 60). We turn now to the passage from A₁ to A₂ — the actualization of perception itself, aisthēsis — which names the specific kinēsis whose unmoved originator is the sensible object exercising its proper quality in actuality, whose moved mover is the sense faculty receiving the sensible form without the matter, and whose terminus is the completed perceptual act together with the dual residual trace it deposits in the ensouled body. This transition is perhaps the decisive hinge of the entire actualization chain, for it is here that the physical world first acquires phenomenal determinacy for the living creature, and here that the material conditions for phantasia and all subsequent cognitive operations are first laid down. Aristotle frames the soul as "a substance in the sense of the form of a natural body" (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. 18), thereby situating the perceptual faculty within the hylomorphic constitution of the organism rather than treating it as a detached cognitive module. The sense faculty, in its first actuality, is a capacity — a hexis or structured readiness — that awaits actualization by an external agent. The sensible object, for its part, possesses its quality in full actuality: the red of the rose, the warmth of the flame, the pitch of the string. When these two first actualities are brought into the appropriate spatial and temporal relation through a properly disposed medium, the transition from A₁ to A₂ occurs. Burke's analysis of motivation in terms of action and substance provides an instructive parallel here, insofar as he insists that terminologies of motion and conditioning are dialectical enterprises designed to clarify the relationship between agent and scene (Burke, *A Grammar of Motives*, pp. 77–80). Similarly, the Aristotelian account of perception is not merely a causal story about physical impingement but a dialectical articulation of how the scene — the sensible environment — and the agent — the perceiving organism — are mutually implicated in a single actualization. What distinguishes the perceptual motion from ordinary physical alteration is precisely its hylomorphic character: the sense faculty receives the form of the sensible object without receiving its matter. This formulation, which has generated extensive scholarly debate, establishes perception as a unique species of alloiōsis, one in which the organ is altered not by taking on the material substrate of the quality but by being assimilated to its formal structure. Gonzalez, examining Aristotle's account of persuasive speech in the *Rhetoric*, emphasizes the reciprocal character of such formal reception, observing that "the orator succeeds when his eunoia and philia are reciprocated by his audience" (Gonzalez, *The Meaning and Function of Phantasia in Aristotle's 'Rhetoric' III.1*, p. 29). Though Gonzalez's immediate concern is rhetorical rather than perceptual, the structural parallel is instructive: just as the orator's goodwill must be received and reciprocated by the audience for persuasion to occur, so too must the sensible form be received and assimilated by the sense organ for perception to be actualized. In both cases, a dyadic relation of active and receptive poles must be brought to completion in a single shared actuality. Gibson, working within a radically different theoretical framework, nonetheless arrives at a convergent insight when he argues that "motion and rest are in fact what an observer experiences with flow and nonflow of the array" (Gibson, *The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception*, pp. 209–210), thereby insisting that perception is not a passive registration of discrete stimuli but an active engagement with the structured affordances of the environment. The sections that follow will trace each moment of this actualization chain in detail, beginning with the preconditions that must obtain before the perceptual act can occur. 

## 2. The Preconditions: A₁ and the Medium

Before the perceptual act can be actualized, two distinct first actualities must be in place: the sensible object must be exercising its proper quality, and the sense organ must possess its capacity in an appropriately disposed state. These twin preconditions constitute A₁, the stage of readiness that precedes but does not yet amount to perception. Aristotle's treatment of this stage is distributed across several passages of the *De Anima*, but its logic is perhaps clearest in his account of the distinction between first and second actuality. The soul, as the first actuality of a natural body potentially having life, stands to the body as the sailor's knowledge of navigation stands to the act of navigating; the capacity is real and fully constituted, yet it awaits an occasion and an object to be exercised (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. 18). Accordingly, the sense faculty in its first-actual state is not merely a bare potentiality — it is not the potentiality of an infant who has never perceived — but a structured readiness, a hexis, that has been informed by the organism's developmental history and is now poised for activation. The sensible object, for its part, must not merely possess its quality dispositionally but must be actively exercising it. Aristotle distinguishes carefully between what is "capable of being seen" and what is "being seen" (Aristotle, *Metaphysics*, pp. 105–106); the former names the first actuality of the visible quality, while the latter names the second actuality in which that quality is fully present to a perceiver. A colored surface in a lightless room possesses the first actuality of visibility without exercising it; only when illuminated and placed within the perceptual field of a suitably disposed organism does the quality pass from dispositional to active presence. This distinction is crucial because it establishes that perception requires a genuine exercise of causal power on the part of the object; the sensible quality is the unmoved mover of the perceptual chain, originating the motion without itself undergoing change. Between object and organ, however, lies the medium — the diaphanous in the case of sight, the air or water in the case of hearing and smell. The medium is not merely an inert conduit through which the sensible form travels; it is itself a necessary precondition, a structural feature of the perceptual situation that must be properly disposed. Aristotle insists that direct contact between object and organ does not produce perception in the case of the distance senses; there must be an intervening medium through which the form is transmitted. Burke, analyzing the scenic dimensions of motivated action, argues that the "circumference of the scene in which occurs the given act" can never be fully delimited, since an act always has a background that extends beyond any particular boundary (Burke, *A Grammar of Motives*, pp. 383–384). The Aristotelian medium functions as precisely such a scenic circumference — an enabling condition that is neither agent nor patient but the field within which the perceptual transaction occurs. Furthermore, as Aristotle notes in his account of incidental perception, "we speak of an incidental object of sense where e.g. the white object which we see is the son of Diares; here because being the son of Diares is incidental to the white which is perceived, we speak of the son of Diares as being incidentally perceived" (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, pp. 25–27). This passage illuminates the layered character of A₁: the proper sensible — whiteness — is what the sense faculty is directly poised to receive, but the total perceptual situation includes incidental features that are co-present without being directly actualized by the sense organ's specific capacity. Gibson's ecological approach offers a modern reformulation of these Aristotelian preconditions. Where Aristotle speaks of the medium as diaphanous — transparent and capable of receiving and transmitting the form of color — Gibson speaks of the ambient optic array as a structured field of light that specifies the surfaces and layouts of the environment (Gibson, *The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception*, pp. 209–210). In both accounts, perception is not a matter of bare stimulus impinging upon a passive receptor but rather a structured encounter between an already organized environment and an already capacitated organism. The medium, whether conceived as Aristotelian diaphanous or as Gibsonian ambient array, is the enabling third term that makes the encounter possible. Thus A₁ names not a single state but a constellation of preconditions — object, medium, and organ — each of which must be in its proper first actuality before the transition to A₂ can commence. 

## 3. Hylomorphism and the Reception of Form

The central and most controversial claim of Aristotle's perceptual theory is that the sense faculty receives the sensible form without the matter. This formulation, which has occasioned a vast literature of interpretation, is the hylomorphic core of the A₁→A₂ transition: it specifies the precise manner in which the sense organ is altered by its encounter with the sensible object. To receive the form without the matter is to undergo a change that is formally but not materially identical with the quality of the object; the eye, in seeing red, does not become materially red in the way that a dye stains cloth, but it does take on the formal structure of redness, becoming, as it were, isomorphic with the quality it perceives. Aristotle defines the soul as "a substance in the sense of the form of a natural body" (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. The hylomorphic account of perception thus distinguishes sharply between ordinary physical alteration — in which one body transmits both form and matter to another, as fire heats and dries wood — and perceptual alteration, in which form alone is transmitted. Nussbaum, in her analysis of phantasia's role in Aristotle's account of action, touches upon the significance of this distinction when she observes that "phantasmata are like aisthemata, only 'without matter'" (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, p. 47). If perception did not involve the reception of form without matter, there would be no basis for the subsequent claim that phantasia preserves formal structures in the absence of their original material substrates; hence the hylomorphic theory of perception is not merely a local doctrine about sense organs but the foundation of Aristotle's entire cognitive psychology. White, situating this doctrine within the broader architectonic of the *De Anima*, identifies the soul's critical power — to kritikon — as the unifying thread that connects perception, phantasia, and thought (White, *The Meaning of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anime, III, 3-8*, pp. 9–11). The soul's capacity to discriminate — to judge that this is white and not black, sweet and not bitter — presupposes that it has received the form of the sensible quality in a manner sufficiently determinate to ground such judgment. The hylomorphic reception of form is thus not a mere passive imprinting but a discriminative event; the sense faculty, in receiving the form, simultaneously exercises its critical capacity to distinguish what it has received. 77–80). In the Aristotelian context, the substance of the sense organ and the action of perceiving are dialectically intertwined; the organ's material constitution conditions what forms it can receive, while the act of reception actualizes both the organ's capacity and the object's quality in a single event. Frede, examining the cognitive role of phantasia, notes that phantasiai have sometimes been "degraded to mere epiphenomena, the lingering after-images of sensations" (Frede, *The Cognitive Role of Phantasia in Aristotle*, p. 3). This characterization, however, rests upon a reductive understanding of the hylomorphic reception that underlies perception: if we take the reception of form without matter seriously, then the formal structure deposited in the sense organ during perception is not an epiphenomenal residue but a genuine ontological determination of the ensouled body. The persistence of this formal determination after the external object is removed is what makes phantasia possible, and it is the hylomorphic character of the original reception that ensures that the persisting trace preserves the formal structure of the perceived quality. Thus the hylomorphic account is indispensable not only for understanding perception itself but for grounding the entire chain of subsequent actualizations — phantasia, memory, deliberation — that depend upon it. Indeed, the very possibility of a dual residual trace, which we shall explore in subsequent sections, rests upon the claim that what perception deposits in the ensouled body is a form, not a material substrate. 

## 4. The Activity of Mover and Moved as One

Aristotle's account of the perceptual act turns upon a principle drawn from the *Physics*: the activity of the mover and the activity of the moved are one and the same activity, though they differ in their being. Motion, as the fulfilment of what is potentially insofar as it is potential, is located in the moved — in the patient — yet it is caused by the agent (Aristotle, *Physics*, p. 60). This principle, when applied to perception, yields the remarkable result that the activity of the sensible object in acting upon the sense organ and the activity of the sense organ in receiving the sensible form are numerically one activity, though they are logically distinguishable as acting and being acted upon. The sound and the hearing are, in their actuality, one and the same event, though the sound is the actuality of the sonorous object and the hearing is the actuality of the auditory organ. Subsequently, the completed perceptual act is neither a property of the object alone nor a property of the organ alone but a shared actuality in which both achieve their second entelecheia simultaneously. This doctrine has profound consequences for the topology of the perceptual event. If the act of the sensible object and the act of the sense organ are one, then perception cannot be adequately described as a chain of discrete causal steps — stimulus, transmission, reception — but must be understood as a single unified event that spans the distance between object, medium, and organ. Burke, analyzing the rhetorical situation in analogous terms, observes that a work's fitness — its decorum — involves a purely technical adaptation of artistic means to artistic end that simultaneously implicates social propriety (Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, p. 149). Similarly, the perceptual act is a technical adaptation of organ to object that simultaneously implicates the broader totality of involvements within which the organism exists. The act is one, but its description requires distinguishing the contributions of agent and patient, just as the description of a rhetorical performance requires distinguishing speaker, speech, and audience even though the persuasive event is a single occurrence. Gonzalez, examining the function of phantasia in rhetoric, underscores this relational character by noting that effective speech depends upon a reciprocity between orator and audience: "the orator succeeds when his eunoia and philia are reciprocated by his audience" (Gonzalez, *The Meaning and Function of Phantasia in Aristotle's 'Rhetoric' III.1*, p. 29). The perceptual analogue is precise: perception succeeds when the sensible object's formal power is reciprocated by the sense organ's receptive capacity. Without this reciprocity, no actualization occurs — the form remains unperceived, the capacity unexercised. The unity of mover and moved in the perceptual act thus establishes a fundamental principle of correlation: the sensible world and the sentient organism are not independent substances that happen to interact but correlative poles of a single actualization, each requiring the other for its full reality to be disclosed. Heidegger's later analysis of Befindlichkeit — the attunement or dispositional state in which Dasein always already finds itself — recasts this Aristotelian insight in existential terms; just as the sense organ must already be disposed to receive the form of the sensible object, so too must Dasein be attuned to a world that has already disclosed itself in a particular mood (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, pp. 113–115). In both cases, receptivity is not passivity but a structured readiness that is constitutive of the perceptual or existential situation. 

## 5. Perception as Enmattered Alloiōsis

Although the reception of form without matter is the defining characteristic of perception, Aristotle is careful to insist that this reception is not a purely formal event detached from the body. Perception is an enmattered alloiōsis — a qualitative alteration that occurs in and through the material constitution of the sense organ. The eye jelly is physically affected by light; the tympanic membrane vibrates in response to sound; the flesh is heated or cooled by the tangible object. These physiological changes are not mere accompaniments of perception but its material substrate; the formal reception could not occur without them. Aristotle's own formulation is unambiguous: the soul is "a substance in the sense of the form of a natural body" that has life potentially (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. 18), and the activities of the soul — including perception — are inseparable from the body whose form it is. Thus perception as enmattered alloiōsis names the inseparability of formal and material dimensions within the perceptual act. Nussbaum draws attention to this enmattered character when she argues that the activities of nous in a living body "must be linked with those of the faculty of phantasia, which it would not be implausible to see as realized in some physiological occurrences" (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, pp. 26–27). If even noetic activity requires a physiological realization through phantasia, then a fortiori perception, which is the causal origin of phantasia, must be thoroughly enmattered. The physiological changes that accompany perception — the warming of the organ, the reception of a particular ratio of qualities — are not accidental but essential features of the perceptual process. Accordingly, the A₁→A₂ transition is not a passage from matter to form but a passage within enmattered form; the organ, already constituted as a determinate material structure with a specific formal capacity, undergoes a further formal determination that alters its material state without destroying its underlying constitution. This conception of perception as enmattered alloiōsis has important consequences for the understanding of the residual trace. If perception involved only the formal reception of a quality without any material alteration, it would be difficult to explain how the sensible form persists in the organ after the external object is removed. But because perception is an enmattered process — because the formal reception is accompanied by and realized in a physiological change — the persistence of the trace is explicable as a material residue of the perceptual event. The physiological alteration persists, and with it the formal structure that it realizes. White's identification of to kritikon as the unifying capacity of the discriminative soul illuminates this point: the soul's power to discriminate — to distinguish white from black, sweet from bitter — is exercised through and in the physiological processes of the sense organs (White, *The Meaning of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anime, III, 3-8*, pp. 9–11). Moreover, Burke's analysis of how "body" in even its "lowliest" forms can be treated as "a way into 'spirit'" rather than as its antithesis provides a conceptual frame for understanding the Aristotelian refusal to separate material and formal dimensions of perception (Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, p. 203). In both frameworks — the Aristotelian and the Burkean — matter and form, body and soul, are not opposed terms but co-constitutive dimensions of a single process. Gibson's ecological psychology similarly resists the separation of perceiver and environment, insisting that the observer's experience of motion and rest is constituted by the optical flow of the ambient array rather than by discrete sensory inputs processed by a disembodied mind (Gibson, *The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception*, pp. 209–210). The doctrine that "optical motion perspective is not the same as visual kinesthesis" implies that what the perceiver encounters is not a representation of the world but the world itself as specified by the structured energy available to the organism. This convergence between Aristotelian enmattered alloiōsis and Gibsonian ecological perception reinforces the claim that the A₁→A₂ transition is an event that occurs at the intersection of organism and environment, form and matter, rather than in a disembodied cognitive space. 

## 6. Resonant Kinēsis: The Persisting Impression

The completion of the perceptual act does not mark the termination of the kinēsis initiated by the sensible object; rather, it deposits a persisting impression in the ensouled body, a residual movement that continues after the object is no longer present. This persisting impression — what Aristotle in the *De Memoria* calls the kinēsis left behind by perception — is the material and formal ground of all subsequent cognitive operations, including memory, phantasia, and deliberation. The nature and status of this residual kinēsis are thus of the highest importance for the actualization chain, for it is through this impression that the completed perceptual act (A₂) becomes the precondition for the next stage of actualization (A₃). Aristotle distinguishes between the perceptual act as a second actuality — the seeing, the hearing, the tasting — and the trace that this act leaves behind. The act itself is temporally bounded; it occurs only so long as the sensible object is present and the medium is properly disposed. But the trace endures. Frede, examining the cognitive role of phantasia, notes that phantasiai have often been treated as "the lingering after-images of sensations" (Frede, *The Cognitive Role of Phantasia in Aristotle*, p. 3). However, as Frede notes, this account does not do justice to the full range of functions that phantasia performs; it reduces the persisting trace to a degraded copy of the original perception rather than recognizing it as a formal determination in its own right (Frede, *The Cognitive Role of Phantasia in Aristotle*, pp. 4–5). The resonant kinēsis is not merely a fading echo but a structured residue that retains the formal character of the original perception while being materially reconstituted in the organ's ongoing physiological activity. White's account of the twofold division of the soul's powers — kinēsis on the one hand, aisthēsis and gnōsis on the other — provides a framework for understanding the resonant character of the persisting impression (White, *The Meaning of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anime, III, 3-8*, p. 8). The residual kinēsis is not a third power of the soul but a modality of the perceptual power itself; it is the perceptual capacity in its after-state, continuing to exercise a diminished form of the discriminative activity that characterizes it in full actuality. This is why Aristotle can say that imagination takes place in the absence of both the faculty and the activity of sense — "imagination takes place in the absence of both, as e.g. in dreams" (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. 42) — without contradicting his claim that phantasia is causally derived from perception. The persisting impression is the bridge between the two: it is the residue of perception that enables imagination to occur in the absence of the original sensible object. Burke's rhetorical analysis illuminates the resonant character of such persisting impressions in a different register. Discussing the strategies by which agents induce themselves and others to act, Burke notes that "men induce themselves and others to act by devices that deduce 'let us' from 'we'" (Burke, *A Grammar of Motives*, pp. 356–358). The rhetorical impression — the dispositional alteration produced by persuasive speech — similarly persists beyond the moment of its original delivery, shaping subsequent deliberation and action. The structural parallel with Aristotle's residual kinēsis is perhaps instructive: in both cases, a temporally bounded act deposits a trace that continues to exert causal influence after the act itself has ceased. The resonance of the impression is not merely a metaphor but a description of the way in which the ensouled body — or, in Burke's terms, the motivated agent — retains and reactivates the formal structures deposited by past encounters. Von Uexküll's concept of Umwelt provides yet another perspective on the persisting impression, one that emphasizes the organism's active constitution of its perceptual world. The Umwelt is not a passive backdrop against which perception occurs but a meaningful environment that the organism constitutes through its perceptual and effectual organs (von Uexkull, *A Foray Into the Worlds of Animals and Humans with A Theory of Meaning*, pp. 222–224). The resonant kinēsis can thus be understood as a modification of the organism's Umwelt: the persisting impression does not merely linger in the organ as a static trace but actively shapes the organism's subsequent encounters with its environment, determining what it notices, what it ignores, and how it responds. Hence, the completion of perception at A₂ is not a terminal event but a generative one, producing the conditions under which the organism's engagement with the world is henceforth altered. 

## 7. The Dual-Trace Thesis: Resonant Aisthēma and Resonant Orexis

The persisting impression left by the completed perceptual act is not a single, undifferentiated residue but a dual trace comprising two distinct yet inseparable moments: the resonant aisthēma (the persisting sensory form) and the resonant orexis (the persisting appetitive valence). Every perception, in Aristotle's account, is simultaneously a discrimination of a sensible quality and an evaluation of that quality as pleasant or painful, beneficial or harmful; accordingly, every perception deposits in the ensouled body both a formal trace of what was perceived and an affective trace of how what was perceived was evaluated. This dual-trace thesis is perhaps the most consequential claim of the A₁→A₂ analysis, for it establishes the joint material and motivational ground from which phantasia, memory, and action subsequently arise. The resonant aisthēma is the formal residue of the sensible quality: the shape, color, sound, or texture that the sense organ received during the perceptual act. Aristotle's account of how "the soul never thinks without a phantasma" — and Nussbaum's observation that "phantasmata are like aisthemata, only 'without matter'" (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, p. 47) — indicates that the aisthēma persists in a form stripped of its original material substrate, subsisting as a formal determination of the organ's ongoing physiological state. This formal persistence is what allows the organism to recall, recognize, and imagine sensible qualities in the absence of the objects that originally produced them. However, the aisthēma does not persist in isolation. Every sensible quality is experienced not merely as a neutral datum but as something that bears upon the organism's well-being; accordingly, the perceptual act also deposits an appetitive valence — a resonant orexis — that marks the perceived quality as desirable or aversive. Aristotle makes this duality explicit in his account of sensitive and deliberative imagination: "Sensitive imagination, as we have said, is found in all animals, deliberative imagination only in those that are calculative: for whether this or that shall be enacted is already a task requiring calculation; and there must be a single standard to measure by, for that is pursued which is greater" (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. 52). The phrase "that is pursued which is greater" reveals the appetitive dimension inherent in even the most basic forms of phantasia: the organism does not merely retain a sensory image but retains it under the aspect of its desirability, measuring it against alternatives. 113–115) — and that they "alter judgements," intruding upon logos in a manner that reveals the inseparability of affect and cognition. The resonant orexis is precisely this intrusion of affect upon form: it is the trace by which every perception carries not only information about the world but a dispositional orientation toward the world. Burke's account of rhetorical motivation enriches this dual-trace analysis. In the *Grammar of Motives*, Burke argues that the fiction of positive law serves to establish "the values, traditions, and trends of business as the Constitution-behind-the-Constitution" (Burke, *A Grammar of Motives*, pp. 383–384), thereby revealing that every act of judgment presupposes a background of evaluative dispositions that are not themselves the objects of explicit deliberation. The resonant orexis functions as a perceptual analogue of Burke's Constitution-behind-the-Constitution: it is the appetitive background against which every subsequent perceptual or cognitive act is evaluated, a background that is itself the product of prior perceptual encounters and their affective residues. Similarly, Burke's observation that "antithesis is so strong a verbal instrument in both rhetoric and dialectic" (Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, p. 203) illuminates the structural logic of the dual trace: the resonant aisthēma and the resonant orexis stand in a relation of complementarity rather than opposition, each requiring the other for the full significance of the perceptual event to be preserved. Frede's careful analysis of the cognitive role of phantasia further supports the dual-trace thesis by noting that the "uncontrolled status of phantasiai as after-images" does not do justice to their role "in memory, thinking, or decision-making" (Frede, *The Cognitive Role of Phantasia in Aristotle*, pp. 4–5). The reason that phantasiai can serve these multiple cognitive functions is precisely that they retain both formal and appetitive dimensions: a memory is not merely the recollection of a sensory image but the recollection of that image as pleasant or painful, significant or trivial; a deliberative phantasma is not merely a picture of a possible future state but a picture charged with desire or aversion. The dual trace deposited by perception thus provides the material from which the entire subsequent cognitive life of the organism is constructed; it is the junction at which the physical world, as formally specified by the sensible object, is first translated into the motivational world of the ensouled body. This account intersects with a productive tension in the corpus between phantasia as causally derived from sensation and phantasia as functionally autonomous in domains such as dreaming, rhetorical reception, memory retention, and involuntary movement. The dual-trace thesis offers a partial resolution of this tension: phantasia is causally derived from perception insofar as the formal and appetitive traces that constitute it are deposited by the perceptual act, but it is functionally autonomous insofar as these traces, once deposited, can be reactivated, recombined, and transformed independently of the original sensible object. The resonant aisthēma and the resonant orexis, taken together, constitute the material basis for this functional autonomy; they are the seeds from which the virtual world of phantasia grows, a world that is rooted in perception but not reducible to it. 

## 8. Synthesis: A₂ as Ground of A₃

The completed perceptual act, together with the dual residual trace it deposits, constitutes A₂ — the second actuality of the perceptual chain and the ground upon which the next stage of actualization, A₃, will be built. A₂ is not merely an endpoint but a threshold: it names the state of the ensouled body after perception has occurred, a state in which the organism carries within itself the formal and appetitive determinations of its encounter with the sensible world. The transition from A₂ to A₃ — from perception to phantasia — will be the subject of the next section of this chapter; here it suffices to establish the precise sense in which A₂ serves as the ground of A₃. First, A₂ supplies the formal content of phantasia. Without the resonant aisthēma deposited by perception, there would be no formal structure for phantasia to preserve, recombine, or transform. Aristotle is explicit on this point: "imagination takes place in the absence of both" the faculty and the activity of sense (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. 42), which means that imagination presupposes a prior perceptual act that has deposited a trace capable of being reactivated. Second, A₂ supplies the appetitive valence that charges phantasia with motivational force. Without the resonant orexis, the phantasma would be a mere formal schema — a picture without significance — rather than the charged image that drives desire, aversion, and deliberation. 77–80); the dual trace deposited by perception ensures that both dimensions are preserved in the passage from A₂ to A₃. Furthermore, A₂ establishes the temporality of the actualization chain. Time, as the number of motion with respect to the before and after, provides the metric within which A₀, A₁, and A₂ are ordered; but A₂ introduces a new temporal dimension, namely the persistence of the trace beyond the moment of its deposition (Aristotle, *Physics*, p. 60). The resonant kinēsis is a temporally extended phenomenon: it is not merely a snapshot of the perceptual act but a continuing modification of the organism's psychophysical state that unfolds over time and is subject to decay, distortion, and reactivation. This temporal extension is what makes memory possible, and it is what distinguishes the Aristotelian account of perception from any model that treats the perceptual act as an instantaneous event without residual consequences. Hence A₂ is not merely the completion of one actualization but the inception of the next — the living hinge between perception and phantasia, between the sensible world and the virtual world that the organism constructs from its perceptual residues. Heidegger's reading of Aristotle's *Rhetoric* on the passions, wherein he identifies pathos as both motion and a cause of motions, a capacity for altering that intrudes upon logos-articulated judgments (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, pp. 113–115), provides the interpretive bridge between the Aristotelian and existential-phenomenological treatments of perceptual receptivity.}

## 9. Development Note

The foregoing analysis of the A₁→A₂ transition — the actualization of perception from its preconditions to its completed act and dual residual trace — has been conducted within a predominantly Aristotelian register, drawing upon the *De Anima*, the *Physics*, and the *Metaphysics* as primary sources. However, the interpretive trajectory of the dissertation as a whole requires that each stage of the actualization chain be placed in dialogue with Heidegger's existential-phenomenological reappropriation of Aristotelian concepts. This development note indicates, in preliminary fashion, how each of the preceding subsections will be taken up in that Heideggerian register in subsequent chapters. With respect to the opening subsection on the actualization of perception (A₁→A₂), Heidegger's treatment of aisthēsis in his 1924 lecture on rhetoric recasts the Aristotelian account as a mode of Dasein's disclosive being-in-the-world, wherein perception is not a cognitive act performed by a subject upon an object but a fundamental manner in which being is disclosed (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, pp. 84–86). With respect to the preconditions (A₁ and the medium), Heidegger's concept of Befindlichkeit — attunement or state-of-mind — re-reads Aristotle's structured readiness of the sense organ as an existential structure in which Dasein always already finds itself disposed toward a world; just as the Aristotelian organ must possess its first actuality as capacity, so too must Dasein be attuned before any particular being can be encountered. With respect to the unity of mover and moved, Heidegger's re-reading of Aristotle's *Physics* III on kinēsis re-interprets the shared actuality of perceiver and perceived as an ontological event in which beings are disclosed within the horizon of being; thus, the unity thesis is radicalized into the claim that being-in-the-world is always already a co-constitutive relation. With respect to perception as enmattered alloiōsis, Heidegger observes that passions are "both motion and a cause of motions" — a "capacity for altering" — and that they "alter judgements," thereby situating the Aristotelian doctrine of perceptual alteration within his own account of how Befindlichkeit shapes logos (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, pp. 113–115). With respect to resonant kinēsis, Heidegger's analysis of the persisting character of mood — the way in which a past attunement continues to condition present disclosure — offers an existential analogue of Aristotle's residual movement. With respect to the dual-trace thesis, the Heideggerian parallel lies in the inseparability of understanding and state-of-mind: every disclosure of beings is simultaneously a cognitive determination and an affective disposition, a dual structure that mirrors the resonant aisthēma and resonant orexis. With respect to the synthesis of A₂ as ground of A₃, Heidegger's account of how past Dasein is retained in the present through historicality — the claim that historiological deficiency does not contradict but rather confirms Dasein's historicality — provides the existential framework for understanding how the perceptual trace grounds subsequent actualizations. Gibson's ecological approach to visual perception, which insists that "the doctrine that vision is exteroceptive, that it obtains 'external' information only, is simply false" (Gibson, *The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception*, pp. 209–210), will serve as a modern empirical counterpoint to both Aristotle's and Heidegger's accounts, bridging the ancient and phenomenological frameworks with a contemporary theory of perception as ecological engagement. Burke's rhetorical theory, particularly his account of identification, consubstantiality, and the scenic determinants of motivated action, will serve as the rhetorical counterpart that links perception, persuasion, and the formation of practical judgment across the entire actualization chain (Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, pp. 93–96). These connections, sketched here in preliminary form, will be developed in full in the chapters that follow. # VALIDATION APPENDIX
